title: Covalent Bonding and the Versatile Carbon

items.title: Today's lesson
items.content:
A diamond ring beside a pencil, and candle wax beside a bowl of salt, open the lesson.

Carbon's four valence electrons lead to **sharing**; electron-dot structures are built from $\mathrm{H_{2}}$, $\mathrm{O_{2}}$ and $\mathrm{N_{2}}$ up to $\mathrm{CH_{4}}$, $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ and $\mathrm{NH_{3}}$.

Why covalent compounds **melt and boil easily** and **do not conduct**; **catenation** and **tetravalency**; and **diamond, graphite and fullerene**.

items.title: You already know
items.content:
• electronic configuration and valence electrons of the first 18 elements

• a full outer shell (8 electrons; 2 for the K shell) is stable

• ionic compounds form by transfer of electrons and have high melting points

items.title: By the end, you can
items.content:
**1.** Explain covalent bonding and draw electron-dot structures for $\mathrm{H_{2}}$, $\mathrm{O_{2}}$, $\mathrm{N_{2}}$, $\mathrm{CH_{4}}$, $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ and $\mathrm{NH_{3}}$.

**2.** Explain why covalent compounds are poor conductors with low melting and boiling points.

**3.** Explain tetravalency and catenation.

**4.** Compare diamond, graphite and fullerene.

items.text:
**What this shows**

Left: a carbon atom, 2 electrons in the first shell and **4 in the outer shell**. Right: the same atom showing only its 4 valence electrons.

**Answer to Question 3**

**Neither is easy.** Gaining four gives $\mathrm{C^{4-}}$: 6 protons would have to hold 10 electrons. Losing four gives $\mathrm{C^{4+}}$: removing four electrons needs a lot of energy.

script.x: Show the carbon atom. Pointer 1 sets it up.
Question 3. Answer is on pointer 2.
Then show the key idea: sharing, the covalent bond, and how × and • are used.

items.text:
**What this shows**

Two hydrogen atoms share **one pair**. × is one atom's electron, • the other's.

**What this shows**

Two oxygen atoms (2, 6). The shared electrons sit **between** the atoms.

**What this shows**

Two nitrogen atoms (2, 5) and the electrons they share.

**Answer to Question 4**

**2**: the shared pair fills its K shell, like helium.

**Answer to Question 5**

**8 each.** Oxygen (2, 6) needs 2 more electrons, so each atom puts in 2: **two shared pairs**, a **double bond**, O=O.

**Answer to Question 6**

**3**: each needs 3 more electrons, a **triple bond**, N≡N.

Show the conclusion box.

items.prompt: Chlorine is 2, 8, 7. Which figure shows the electron-dot structure of a chlorine molecule, $\mathrm{Cl_{2}}$?

items.text:
**On this question**

**B**: each chlorine needs 1 electron, so they share **one pair**; each then has 8. (A) shares two pairs, (C) transfers an electron (ionic), and (D) leaves each chlorine with only 6.

script.x: Activate the question: the four figures are its options. Explain depending on time available.
Pointer 1 carries the reasoning.

items.text:
**What this shows**

Electron-dot structures (top) and bond lines (bottom) of methane, water and ammonia. × is the central atom's electron, • hydrogen's.

Methane, $\mathrm{CH_{4}}$, is a fuel and the main part of biogas and CNG.

**Answer to Question 7**

Each hydrogen shares 1 electron. Carbon needs 4 more, nitrogen 3 and oxygen 2, so they share **4, 3 and 2 pairs**. The number of electrons an atom shares is its **valency**.

**Answer to Question 8**

**2**, one unshared pair. **Yes**: 3 shared pairs (6) + 2 = **8**.

script.x: Show the key idea: from molecules of one element to compounds. Then the three structures. Pointer 1 sets them up.
Questions 7 and 8. Answers are on pointers 2 and 3.
Show the conclusion box, pointing back to the three structures.

items.prompt: The figure shows the electron-dot structure of carbon dioxide, $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$. Is each bond single, double or triple?

items.text:
**On this question**

**B**: carbon shares **2 pairs** (4 electrons) with each oxygen: two **double bonds**, O=C=O. Each oxygen also keeps 2 unshared pairs, so every atom has 8.

items.text:
**What this shows**

Melting and boiling points (in kelvin) of four carbon compounds and of sodium chloride, which is ionic.

**Answer to Question 9**

**Acetic acid** (melts at 290 K), **chloroform** and **ethanol** are liquids; **methane** boils at 111 K, so it is a **gas**. Sodium chloride is a solid.

script.x: Show the table. Pointer 1 sets it up.
Question 9. Answer is on pointer 2.

items.text:
**What this shows**

Ions in **sodium chloride**: each ion is strongly attracted by the ions around it. There are no molecules.

**Answer to Question 10**

The electrons are **shared** between atoms, so **no ions** (charged particles) are formed to carry the current.

**What this shows**

Separate **methane molecules**. Each line inside a molecule is a covalent bond; the dotted lines are the forces **between** molecules.

**Answer to Question 11**

Boiling only pulls the **molecules away from one another**; the bonds inside each molecule are not broken. The forces **between** molecules are **weak**, so little energy is needed.

Question 11. Answer is on pointer 4.
Show the conclusion box.

items.prompt: Compound P melts at 1074 K and conducts electricity when molten. Compound Q melts at 290 K and does not conduct when molten. Which is covalent, and why?
options: Q: low melting point and no ions
P: high melting point and it conducts
Q: it melts at a high temperature
P: covalent compounds conduct when molten

items.text:
**On this question**

**A**: Q's **low melting point** shows weak forces between molecules, and it does not conduct because it has **no ions**. P is ionic.

items.text:
**What this shows**

Ways in which carbon atoms join: (a) a straight chain, (b) a branched chain, (c) a ring; and single, double and triple bonds.

**Answer to Question 12**

Carbon atoms are bonded to **other carbon atoms**: in straight chains, branched chains and rings, by single, double or triple bonds.

items.text:
**Answer to Question 13**

**3 each**, filled by hydrogen atoms. **7 bonds**: 1 C—C + 6 C—H.

items.prompt: Silicon (2, 8, 4) is also tetravalent. Why does it not form as many compounds as carbon?
options: Its catenation is limited: chains of bigger atoms are short and reactive
It has no valence electrons to share
Its bonds are stronger than carbon's

items.text:
**On this question**

**A**: silicon chains are only up to **seven or eight atoms** long and are very reactive. Silicon atoms are **bigger**, so their bonds are weaker.

items.text:
**What this shows**

The arrangement of carbon atoms in (a) **diamond** and (b) **graphite**. Each ball is a carbon atom; each line is a bond.

**Answer to Question 14**

**Diamond: 4**, in a rigid three-dimensional structure, so it is the **hardest** natural substance.

**Graphite: 3**, in flat hexagonal **layers** stacked one above another; the layers are held **weakly** and **slide** over each other, so graphite is smooth and slippery.

items.prompt: Name the allotrope of carbon: (i) used in pencils and as electrodes, (ii) used to cut glass and drill through rock, (iii) shaped like a football.

items.text:
**On this question**

**A**: (i) **graphite** (soft, conducts), (ii) **diamond** (hardest), (iii) **fullerene** ($\mathrm{C_{60}}$).
